concept.name: Triple top
concept.definition: A classical bearish reversal pattern in which price in an uptrend tests the same resistance level three times, forming three roughly equal, well-spaced highs, and completes only when price breaks below the pattern's support (the lowest of the intervening lows). It extends the double-top logic: three rejections of the same supply zone. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Three failed attempts to push through the same ceiling exhaust the buyers; once the floor between those attempts gives way, there are no buyers left to hold the level.
concept.mechanics: Require a prior uptrend, three comparable highs (not exactly equal but reasonably close) marking clear turning points, typically forming over three to six months, with volume usually declining through the pattern. Confirmation is a break below the lowest intervening low, reinforced by volume expansion; the support break often turns into resistance on a retest. The target subtracts the pattern height from the support break.
concept.formula: Price target = S - (H - S), where H = average high of the three peaks and S = the support level (lowest intervening low) at the break.
concept.failure_modes: Until support breaks, the pattern is indistinguishable from a neutral rectangle or even a bullish ascending triangle, and an upside breakout through the triple resistance produces a powerful continuation instead. Rare, textbook-perfect triple tops tempt over-fitting to imperfect real charts.
concept.misconceptions: That three equal highs are by themselves bearish — three equal highs also appear in rectangles and ascending triangles, so the pattern should be treated as neutral until the downside break occurs.
concept.example: A stock in an uptrend fails three times near $23 over four months, then breaks below the $19.80 support from the May low on expanding volume, projecting a decline toward $16.60.
